incidents.title: TTFT spike after a deploy
incidents.opening: At 14:05 the p99 time-to-first-token alert fired for the chat endpoint in eu-north. Users say the model 'thinks' for several seconds before it starts to answer. You are on call. Go.

questions.answer: All tenants on the eu-north chat endpoint. No errors, only slow first tokens. p99 TTFT is 4.1 s against a normal 0.6 s. p50 is 0.9 s against 0.5 s. Support has six tickets.
Request rate is flat. Error rate is 0.1%. TTFT is up and end-to-end latency is up. Inter-token latency is flat at about 25 ms. The waiting queue per replica rose from about 2 to about 30 at 13:55.
A deploy finished at 13:50. It moved the router and the engine image together to all 12 replicas in ten minutes. There was no canary stage. The values file was also rewritten.
vllm:num_requests_waiting is about 30 per replica. Running requests sit at the batch cap.
vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc is about 0.45. No preemption lines in the engine logs. No out-of-memory events.
vllm:prefix_cache_hits divided by vllm:prefix_cache_queries fell from about 0.55 to about 0.03 at 13:52. The chat product sends the same 3,000-token system prompt on every request.
GPU utilisation rose from about 70% to about 95%. The extra work is prefill.
The input and output length distributions are unchanged from yesterday.
All 12 replicas look the same. It is not one bad pod.
No errors and no restarts. The logs show only normal request lines.
The new router config lost the prefix-hash routing setting. Requests with the same prompt prefix are now spread across all replicas by round robin.

incidents.root_cause: The deploy removed prefix-aware routing. The prefix cache hit rate collapsed, every request redoes the 3,000-token prefill, and the queue grows.

destructive.why: restarting every replica at once empties every KV and prefix cache at the same moment, so TTFT gets worse

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Roll back the deploy now with kubectl rollout undo, then watch TTFT and the prefix cache hit rate recover. Diff the values file afterwards.
scoring_notes: Strong answers ask what changed before touching anything.
Scaling out is not a fix. New replicas start with an empty prefix cache.

incidents.title: GPU pool shrinking silently
incidents.opening: No alert fired. A customer on a dedicated endpoint says latency has crept up for three days and one request in fifty now times out. Your Kubernetes dashboard says everything is healthy. Go.

questions.answer: One dedicated endpoint, eight replicas of one model, one tenant. p99 latency rose from 2.0 s to 6.5 s over three days. About 2% of requests time out at peak.
Kubernetes view: desired 8, ready 8, no alerts. The per-replica request view shows only five replicas receiving traffic. Three show zero. The five run at 95% of their batch cap.
No deploy for two weeks. A node pool maintenance event three days ago drained and replaced two GPU nodes.
kubectl get pods shows all eight Running and Ready. Three pods show 38, 41 and 44 restarts since the maintenance event. The other five show 0.

Events on the restarting pods say the liveness probe failed and the container will be restarted. The probe is an HTTP check with a 1 s timeout and a failure threshold of 1. During a large prefill the engine answers slowly.

The router admin view lists five registered workers. The three missing are the three restarting pods. Router logs say worker registration failed, upstream not ready, and no retry. Workers register once at startup.
Readiness passes on all eight pods after warm-up. Kubernetes counts them as ready even though the router does not know about three of them.
Five GPUs busy at about 90%. Three idle after the first minute following each restart.
Existing alerts watch pod readiness and the error rate. Nothing compares router pool size with desired replicas.
The endpoint is set to min 8 and max 8 replicas. There is no spare.

incidents.root_cause: An aggressive liveness probe restarts healthy workers during long prefills. After each restart the worker registers with the router once, fails, and never rejoins. Kubernetes says 8 of 8 while the router serves from 5.

destructive.why: restarting or deleting the whole pool removes the five workers that are still serving

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Get the three workers back into the router one at a time, loosen the liveness probe so it stops killing busy workers, and add an alert on router pool size against desired replicas.
scoring_notes: Strong answers notice that ready in Kubernetes and registered in the router are two different facts.
Do not remove the probes. Loosen the liveness probe and keep readiness.

incidents.title: KV-cache pressure and a 429 storm
incidents.opening: The 429 rate on a dedicated endpoint is 22% and rising, and p99 latency has tripled. Traffic is 35% above the usual peak. Product asks whether to raise the rate limits. Go.

questions.answer: One dedicated endpoint, one model, three tenants. 22% of requests return 429. Tenants B and C are complaining. Tenant A is not.
Request rate is up 35%. 429 is 22%. Waiting queue per replica is about 70. KV cache usage is 98 to 100% on all six replicas. Pool output tokens per second fell 40% while requests rose.
No deploy. Tenant A went live with a document-summarisation feature at 10:40.
The gateway per-tenant limits are not hit and the remaining-quota headers look healthy. The 429s come from the router, which sheds load when every worker's queue is over its depth limit.
KV usage is pinned at 98 to 100%. Engine logs show many preemptions. Preempted requests go back to the waiting queue and prefill again.
Tenant A sends prompts of about 28,000 tokens at about 5 requests per second. Other tenants send about 1,000 tokens. The model allows 32,000.
Output tokens per second are down 40%. GPU utilisation is high. The GPUs are redoing work after preemptions.
SDK clients retry a 429 up to three times and ignore Retry-After. Retries are about 30% of arrivals.
Tenant A limit is 600 requests per minute and 10,000,000 tokens per minute. They use about 300 RPM and 8.4 million TPM, so they are inside both.
Max replicas is 10 and six are running. A new replica takes about 12 minutes to become ready.

incidents.root_cause: One tenant's 28,000-token prompts exhaust the KV cache. The engine preempts and recomputes, throughput collapses, the queues fill, and the router sheds load. Client retries add to the storm.

destructive.why: the router shedding is protecting the pool, and removing it turns 429s into timeouts and out-of-memory kills
a restart empties all in-flight work and makes the 429s worse

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Cap the long-prompt tenant by tokens per minute or concurrent long requests, start scaling out knowing it takes 12 minutes, ask clients to honour Retry-After, and tell tenant A what you did.
scoring_notes: Strong answers separate who returns the 429 from why. A request-per-minute limit cannot see a long prompt. A token limit can.
Saying 'raise the limits' is the wrong instinct. The pool is full.

incidents.title: Regional partial outage with retry amplification
incidents.opening: Error rate on the eu-west regional endpoint is 15% and climbing. User traffic is flat. Gateways are at three times their normal CPU. Upstream request rate is four times the user request rate. Go.

questions.answer: eu-west only, all tenants. 15% of requests fail with 503 or time out. eu-north is fine. These tenants are bound to EU data residency.

Three zones, a, b and c. Zone b workers show errors and timeouts. Zones a and c are healthy but their queues are growing. User traffic is 1,000 requests per second. Gateway-to-router attempts are 4,000 per second.
No deploys. The cloud provider status page shows a degraded network in zone b that started ten minutes ago.

The SDK retries up to three times. The gateway retries failed upstream calls up to three times. The router retries on another worker up to three times. There is no retry budget. Backoff is a fixed 100 ms with no jitter.
Zone b holds 4 of 12 workers, all failing health checks intermittently on the network. Zones a and c hold 8 workers at 92% KV usage because they absorb the retries.
Zones a and c can carry the real user load at about 85% of capacity if the retries stop. They cannot carry user load plus four times the attempts.
eu-north has 15% headroom. A teammate proposes sending the overflow to the US region, which is idle. The affected tenants are bound to EU residency.
Liveness probes on zone b workers flap. Kubernetes restarts some, and they come back and fail again.
You can set the zone b weight to zero at the load balancer with one command.
Client, gateway and router timeouts are all 60 seconds.

incidents.root_cause: A degraded zone b network started the failures. Unbudgeted retries at three layers multiplied the load, up to 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 attempts per user request, so the healthy zones saturated and a partial outage became a regional one.

destructive.why: moving EU-resident traffic to the US region breaks the data residency promise
restarting or adding gateways adds more retry load and drops in-flight work

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Stop the amplification first by cutting or budgeting retries at the gateway and router. Drain zone b at the load balancer. Shed load early if zones a and c still saturate. Keep traffic inside the EU.
scoring_notes: Strong answers name the multiplication across layers and say which layer to cut first.
Data residency is a hard constraint. Name it before anyone suggests a US failover.

incidents.title: Model weights download stuck at cold start
incidents.opening: The autoscaler added four replicas of a 70B model 25 minutes ago because the existing four are saturated. None is Ready. The new pods show 0/1 and a rising restart count. Go.

questions.answer: One dedicated endpoint. Four ready replicas at 97% KV usage. p99 latency is up 2x and 5% of requests return 429. Traffic is a morning peak, 40% over yesterday.
Desired 8, ready 4. Waiting queue about 40 per ready replica. New pods are Running 0/1 with two or three restarts each.
No deploy. The autoscaler fired on queue depth. The four new pods landed on two GPU nodes that joined the pool 30 minutes ago.
Pod logs say downloading shard 12 of 30. Then nothing for minutes. Then the container is killed and the log starts again at shard 1.
Events say the startup probe failed and the container will be restarted. The startup probe allows 10 minutes in total. The last termination reason is not out of memory.
Each pod pulls at about 20 MB per second. The model is about 140 GB in 30 shards.
The object store sends occasional throttle responses. The downloader backs off for a long time after each one.
Weights are fetched from the object store at every container start into the container's own writable layer. There is no node-local cache and no shared volume. The new nodes have nothing warm.
Last week's scale-out used a node image with the weights pre-pulled and took about 6 minutes. The new nodes use the plain image.

incidents.root_cause: The new nodes have no local copy of the weights. A pod needs about 140,000 MB at 20 MB per second, which is 7,000 seconds or about two hours. The startup probe kills it at ten minutes and the download restarts from shard 1.

destructive.why: deleting a pod restarts the download from shard 1, and more pods share the same slow object store path

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Stop the restart loop by giving the startup probe enough time, protect the four ready replicas with load shedding or per-tenant limits, and fix the cold start with a pre-pulled or shared weights volume.
scoring_notes: Strong answers do the arithmetic: 140 GB at 20 MB per second is about two hours, far past a ten-minute probe.
Adding more replicas makes it worse. Say why.

incidents.title: Disk full on a GPU node
incidents.opening: Alert: DiskPressure on GPU node gpu-17. Two pods were evicted. A vLLM replica on it restarted and now crashes at start with 'No space left on device'. Get the node healthy. Go.

questions.answer: One node of a 40-node pool. One of 8 replicas of a dedicated endpoint is down. The endpoint serves on 7 of 8 with latency up 15%.
Node view: root filesystem 100% used. CPU and memory normal. Other nodes under 60% disk.
Last night an engineer set VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG on that replica to chase a stall. The Deployment was patched at 22:00.
df -h: 100G size, 100G used, 0 available, 100%. df -i: 12% of inodes used.
du -xh --max-depth=2 /var shows /var/log/pods 18 GB and /var/lib/containerd 22 GB. That is about 40 GB, far less than the 100 GB that df reports as used.
lsof +L1 shows the engine process holding /var/log/vllm/engine.log (deleted), 58 GB. A cleanup cron removed the file at 02:00. The process still writes to it.
describe node shows the DiskPressure condition true. The kubelet evicted two low-priority batch pods.
/var/lib/containerd holds images and a 22 GB model cache that running replicas on the node use right now.
Other pods on the node serve traffic. You may cordon the node.

incidents.root_cause: Debug logging wrote 58 GB to a file that a cleanup job then deleted. The process still holds it open, so the space is not freed. du cannot see the file. df can.

destructive.why: wiping images and the model cache slows recovery and does not free the file that is held open

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Cordon the node, free the held file by restarting its holder or truncating through /proc, turn debug logging off, then add a disk alert and fix the cleanup job.
scoring_notes: Strong answers use the du versus df gap as the clue and say why it points to a deleted but open file.
Check inodes too. Here they are fine, which rules out inode exhaustion.

incidents.title: Certificate expiry
incidents.opening: At 09:00 UTC the support queue fills with 'certificate has expired' from clients calling the public API. Your internal dashboards load fine. Go.

questions.answer: All external clients of api.example.test in every region fail. Internal traffic is fine. Clients that skip verification still work.
Request rate from strict clients fell to near zero at 09:00:00. Backend error rate is 0 because requests never arrive. The edge shows TLS handshake failures.
No deploy. Nothing changed at 09:00 except the clock.
openssl x509 -noout -enddate on the served certificate gives notAfter=Nov 9 08:59:59 2026 GMT. It was issued 90 days ago by an ACME CA through cert-manager.
kubectl describe certificate shows Ready False. Renewal attempts have failed for 30 days. The order fails at the DNS-01 challenge with an authentication error from the DNS provider API.
The DNS provider API token used by the solver was rotated 31 days ago in the secrets manager. The cluster secret still holds the old token.
No alert on days to expiry. cert-manager failures were not routed to anyone.
kubeadm certs check-expiration shows the control plane certificates with over 200 days left. A wildcard certificate for the console expires in 6 days and uses the same renewal path.
With a working token you can request a certificate manually and load it into the TLS Secret. The ingress controller reloads Secret changes.

incidents.root_cause: The renewal has failed for 30 days because a rotated DNS provider token was never updated in the cluster. Nothing alerted on days to expiry.

destructive.why: telling clients to skip verification removes the protection the certificate gives and trains them to ignore it
deleting the Secret makes the ingress fall back to a default certificate and the cert-manager docs do not recommend it for rotation

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Update the DNS provider token, force a renewal with cmctl renew, verify from outside with openssl s_client, install an emergency manual certificate if renewal is slow, then fix the six-day certificate and add an expiry alert.
scoring_notes: Strong answers check the second certificate that expires in six days.
Never tell customers to turn verification off.

incidents.title: DNS: intermittent resolution failures
incidents.opening: Gateway pods log 'Temporary failure in name resolution' on about one request in twenty. It began 20 minutes ago. Overall traffic is normal. Go.

questions.answer: The gateway in one cluster. About 5% of requests fail with 502 because the token validation call cannot resolve its host. The inference path itself works.
Gateway errors 5%. CoreDNS has two replicas with CPU at the limit and throttled. Query rate is 12,000 per second, up from 3,000. DNS latency p99 is up to 2 s and some queries time out.
A gateway release at 10:05 added a per-request call to an external identity provider, idp.example.test.
The pod's /etc/resolv.conf has nameserver 10.0.0.10, three search domains and options ndots:5.
With the CoreDNS log plugin briefly on: for each lookup of idp.example.test the pod first asks for the name with each search suffix. Those return NXDOMAIN. Then the real name is asked.
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns shows two Running. The CPU limit is 200m and the pods are throttled.
There is no NodeLocal DNSCache.
The upstream resolver is healthy. Queried directly from a node it answers in 5 ms.
From a dnsutils pod, nslookup kubernetes.default works but sometimes takes 1.5 s. An external name alone sometimes times out.

incidents.root_cause: The new per-request lookup of an external name, with ndots 5, multiplies each lookup into several queries. Throttled CoreDNS replicas cannot keep up, so some queries time out.

destructive.why: removing every CoreDNS pod at once breaks DNS for the whole cluster, and hard-coded hosts entries go stale

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Reduce the load: roll back or flag off the new lookup, scale CoreDNS and lift its CPU limit, and use a fully qualified name with a trailing dot or a lower ndots through dnsConfig. Plan NodeLocal DNSCache afterwards.
scoring_notes: Strong answers explain why one lookup becomes several queries.
Test from a pod, not from your laptop. Pod DNS has its own resolver settings.

incidents.title: etcd latency
incidents.opening: kubectl get takes eight seconds. Rollouts and the autoscaler are stalling. The API server logs 'etcdserver: request timed out'. Inference traffic is still being served. Go.

questions.answer: The control plane is degraded. Running pods keep serving. New pods are not created, autoscaling decisions are late and node status updates lag. If traffic spikes, the cluster cannot add capacity.

API server p99 request latency is 8 s. etcd had 6 leader changes in 30 minutes. wal_fsync_duration_seconds p99 is 180 ms on member 2 and about 6 ms on the others. Member 2 is the leader most of the time.
No deploys. A nightly backup job started at 02:00. The incident began at 02:05.
etcd logs on member 2 say failed to send out heartbeat on time and apply entries took too long. Leader elections follow.
iostat on member 2 shows the device at 100% utilisation with high write await. Member 2 shares that disk with API server logs, and the backup job writes a 40 GB copy to the same device.
Database size is 3.1 GB against an 8 GB quota. etcdctl alarm list shows no alarms.
Three members, all healthy, quorum intact. Only member 2 is slow.
etcd runs colocated with the API server on three control-plane VMs.
Round trip between members is under 1 ms with no packet loss.

incidents.root_cause: The nightly backup writes 40 GB to the same disk as the etcd leader's write-ahead log. Fsync latency is 180 ms against the 10 ms the etcd FAQ asks for, so heartbeats are missed and leadership flaps.

destructive.why: defragmenting a live member blocks reads and writes, and restarting or removing members forces more elections

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Stop the backup job competing for the leader's disk, confirm fsync p99 and leader changes settle, then move the backup to its own disk or throttle it. Do not defragment or restart members during the incident.
scoring_notes: Strong answers say that running pods keep serving but nothing can change, and what that means for autoscaling.
Defragmentation is the classic wrong move. It blocks the member.

incidents.title: Bad config push
incidents.opening: It is 11:44. The 5xx rate at the API gateway is 100% in eu-north and climbing in eu-west. A config sync from the GitOps automation finished at 11:42. You are on call. Go.

questions.answer: All tenants in eu-north see 100% 503. eu-west is at 30% and rising. The US regions are not affected yet.
The gateway returns 503 with no healthy upstream for every model. Workers are healthy and idle. The request rate reaching workers in eu-north dropped to zero.

Yes. A config sync at 11:42 changed the routing table. It rolled to eu-north, then eu-west at 11:44, and the US regions are scheduled for 11:50. There is no canary stage. A bot account merged it from a generator.

The generated routing file has an empty upstreams list for every model. The generator read an empty service-discovery export and treated it as no workers. Validation passed because an empty list is valid.
The sync can be paused with one click in the GitOps controller. The next region is scheduled in six minutes.
The previous commit is known good and was deployed three days ago.
You have cluster access and the GitOps UI is up.
Workers are healthy and ready with no restarts.

incidents.root_cause: A generator turned an empty service-discovery export into a routing table with no upstreams. The pipeline had no canary, so the empty list reached every region in minutes.

destructive.why: editing live config fights the GitOps controller, which will overwrite it, and deleting the gateway removes the last working pieces

incidents.ideal_mitigation: Pause the sync before the next region, revert to the last known good commit through the same pipeline, verify the 503 rate falls in each region, then add validation and a canary stage.
scoring_notes: Stopping the spread comes before the revert. Strong answers say both in that order.
Fix forward is wrong under pressure. Revert.
